plan:
EXPERIMENT DESIGN — Does chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting improve task-solving ability of LLM-based agents in WorkArena++?
(Design only. Nothing below has been executed; no results are claimed. Workspace inspection confirmed /workspace contains no benchmark code, scaffolding, or datasets — only task.json declaring this design-only track — so all implementation specifics are stated as assumptions.)

====================================================
1. RESEARCH QUESTION AND HYPOTHESES
====================================================
Q: Does CoT prompting improve the task-solving ability of LLM-based agents in WorkArena++?

H1 (primary): Mean per-task success rate under CoT prompting > under no-CoT prompting on WorkArena++ tasks.
H2 (stratified): The CoT effect differs by task family/difficulty — predicted (as a hypothesis to test, not a fact) to be larger on reasoning and planning tasks than on compositional tasks.
H3 (mechanism/moderator): The effect depends on the CoT operationalization (zero-shot vs. interleaved per-step) and on model capability (smaller/stronger models may differ in whether CoT helps or hurts), and CoT may increase steps/token cost — a potential benefit-at-a-cost tradeoff.

DESIGN DECISION (not a fact): "CoT" is ambiguous in agentic settings. This design operationalizes it as TWO distinct arms — zero-shot CoT and interleaved per-step CoT — rather than presuming one mechanism. If the researcher later must name a single mechanism, the decision should default to interleaved per-step CoT (closest to how CoT manifests in browser-agent loops), but the primary analysis treats them as separate arms against the shared no-CoT baseline.

====================================================
2. ARMS AND MANIPULATION (Independent variable)
====================================================
Four arms, identical in everything except prompt text:

A1. No-CoT (direct): Instruction directs the agent to act/answer directly, e.g., "Complete the task using the browser tools. Act directly; do not provide extended deliberation."
A2. Zero-shot CoT: A1 + a single appended instruction, e.g., "Before acting, think step by step: state your plan, identify the relevant UI elements and the information you need, then act." Reasoning is elicited once; the scaffold does not otherwise constrain intermediate output.
A3. Interleaved per-step CoT: The scaffold's system prompt requires, at EVERY agent step, a short structured reasoning block (current goal → observed page state → candidate action → justification) before emitting the action; e.g., "At each step, first write 1–3 sentences of reasoning about the current state and your next action, then output the action." Implementation in the scaffold: the agent loop is modified so each LLM call's output is parsed into a REASON field followed by an ACTION field; the REASON field is shown to the model in subsequent turns (it is part of the trajectory) but the ACTION parsers/validators are unchanged. This makes per-step CoT a prompt-level manipulation, not an architecture change.
A4. Matched-length control: A1's text padded with neutral, task-irrelevant filler of approximately equal token count to the CoT instruction used in A2 (and a second variant matched to A3's cumulative per-step overhead where practical). Purpose: separate "more instruction tokens / longer prompts" from "reasoning elicitation." (If budget forces a choice, A4 is matched to A2, the cheapest control, and A3's overhead is reported descriptively.)

Implementation notes: all arms share one agent scaffold (single codebase, single agent loop, same tool set, same observation format, same termination logic, same error/retry handling). The only delta between arms is the instruction text and (for A3) the REASON-then-ACTION output format. Prompt templates are version-controlled and pre-registered before the run. A blind labeling scheme (arm IDs unrelated to content) is used when coding failure modes.

DESIGN DECISION: A2 and A3 are kept as separate arms rather than collapsing them, because zero-shot CoT is the literature-standard probe while interleaved CoT is the more ecologically valid agentic form; conflating them would make any effect uninterpretable.

====================================================
3. TASKS, TASKSETS, AND STRATIFICATION
====================================================
Benchmark: WorkArena++ (compositional, reasoning, and planning task families over knowledge-worker workflows in a ServiceNow instance; per-task automatic validators).

Task sampling: A fixed, pre-registered task set sampled from each of the three families at each available difficulty level, stratified so each family × difficulty cell is represented. Default plan (assumption permitting): sample the full task inventory if the instance supports seeded generation; otherwise a stratified random sample of ~100–150 tasks per family (≈300–450 tasks total), with the exact stratum counts fixed before any run. Tasks are the SAME instances across all arms (paired design). Where instance seeding supports randomization, each task×run uses a different instance seed; where it does not, tasks are reused identically and seeds vary only decoding/trajectory stochasticity (see Assumption A4).

Counterbalancing: Task order within each run is randomized; each task is attempted by all arms, and the task×arm schedule is shuffled so any time-varying instance state cannot systematically favor one arm.

Seeds: Per task and arm, R independent runs with distinct decoding seeds (default R = 3; sensitivity analysis at R = 1 and R = 5 in the power section below). Success is scored per run; the per-task outcome is the run-level binary result (all runs analyzed, not just the first).

====================================================
4. CONTROLS (what is held fixed)
====================================================
Identical across arms: model(s) and model version pinning; decoding parameters (temperature, top-p, max tokens); system prompt except the manipulated text; tool/action set and tool descriptions; observation truncation and screenshot settings; maximum steps per episode and token/cost budget per episode; termination and stall rules; validator/checker code and success criteria; ServiceNow instance configuration and dataset version; hardware/host configuration; run schedule and order randomization.
Randomization: task order shuffled per run; arm schedule counterbalanced across tasks.
Blinding: failure-mode annotation performed on arm-deidentified logs.
Leakage guard: the no-CoT prompt must not contain any instruction that elicits planning or reasoning; the matched-length control ensures added tokens alone don't produce the effect.
Contamination guard: prompts are checked to ensure CoT wording does not inadvertently hint at task solutions (it contains no task-specific content).

====================================================
5. OUTCOME MEASURES
====================================================
Primary: per-task binary success as determined by WorkArena++'s own validators, scored per (task, arm, run). Reported overall and stratified by family (compositional / reasoning / planning) and difficulty level.
Secondary: (a) steps-to-termination; (b) total tokens and dollar/API cost per episode; (c) wall-clock time; (d) failure-mode taxonomy coded from trajectory logs: stalled/looped behavior, wrong-element interaction, missed validator condition, exceeded step budget, formatting/parse errors, and (for A3 specifically) degenerate or template-like reasoning text. (e) Optionally, a blind qualitative rating of reasoning quality on a subsample to check that A3 reasoning is substantive rather than boilerplate.

====================================================
6. ANALYSIS PLAN
====================================================
6.1 Primary test. Paired analysis at the task level: for each task, aggregate run-level successes per arm (proportion of successful runs). Fit a mixed-effects logistic regression: success ~ arm + family + difficulty + arm×family + arm×difficulty + (1|task) + (1|run seed), with A1 as reference. Report adjusted odds ratios and 95% CIs for A2 vs. A1, A3 vs. A1, A4 vs. A1, and A2 vs. A3. Complement with a paired permutation/bootstrap test on the per-task success difference (task-level paired bootstrap, e.g., 10,000 resamples) for a design-free robustness check. Family-wise control: pre-specify the two primary contrasts (A2 vs. A1 and A3 vs. A1) at α = .05 with Holm correction; all other contrasts are exploratory.
6.2 Stratified analysis: report per-family and per-difficulty success rates with CIs; test the arm×family interaction (H2). Pre-specify the directional prediction (larger CoT gains on reasoning/planning) so it is a test, not a post-hoc story.
6.3 Secondary metrics: steps and tokens analyzed with analogous mixed models (e.g., Gamma/negative-binomial or rank-based tests); failure-mode proportions compared per arm with the same task-level pairing.
6.4 Power / sample-size reasoning (tied to assumed budget). Design effect of pairing: paired comparisons on ~300–450 tasks with R = 3 runs give strong power for moderate effects. Roughly: to detect a 10-point absolute success-rate difference (e.g., 40% → 50%) with ~80% power at α = .05 (two-sided, paired), on the order of ~150–200 tasks are needed under conservative within-task correlation assumptions; ~300+ tasks comfortably detect 5–8 point differences. Under the default budget (§7) the design is powered for ≥10-point overall differences and can detect the predicted family-level interactions only if the effect is moderate (≥15 points within a family); this is stated a priori so a null on a small stratum is not over-interpreted. If budget is halved, the design stays powered for ~12–15 point differences overall and loses interaction power — in that case family-level analyses become descriptive.
6.5 Robustness: (i) repeat primary analysis excluding tasks with any validator ambiguity; (ii) repeat excluding the first run per task (warm-up effects); (iii) sensitivity to episode step-budget cap (if truncation rates differ across arms, re-run with a larger cap on a subsample); (iv) per-model replication if multiple models are used.

====================================================
7. MODELS AND BUDGET (assumption-dependent)
====================================================
Default: two models — one strong frontier-class API model and one smaller/weaker model — to test whether the CoT effect is capability-dependent (H3); a single-model fallback if budget is constrained. Cost model per arm: episodes × steps × tokens/step × model price. Rough default budget: 4 arms × ~300–450 tasks × 3 runs × ≤25 steps ≈ 9k–16k episodes per model; at typical API pricing this is the dominant cost driver and should be sanity-checked against the researcher's actual budget before finalizing task counts (see uncertainties). Runtime: browser-agent episodes are the wall-clock bottleneck; runs are parallelizable across tasks, and the full matrix is feasible in days, not weeks, with modest parallelism (assumption: sufficient parallel API quota and instance capacity).

====================================================
8. FEASIBILITY AND ASSUMPTIONS (each stated with sensitivity if wrong)
====================================================
Workspace finding: /workspace contains only task.json; no WorkArena++ code, scaffolding, prompt templates, or benchmark data are present, and the environment has no network or preinstalled ML dependencies. This is consistent with the design-only track, but it means every executable element below is an assumption, not a verified capability.

A1. ServiceNow test instance availability. WorkArena++ tasks execute against a ServiceNow instance with seeded data. If unavailable, the experiment cannot run as designed; sensitivity: high — this is the single gating assumption. Fallback: none faithful (mocked UI would change task difficulty and validator semantics).
A2. Benchmark harness + agent scaffold availability (WorkArena++/BrowserGym-style code with per-task validators). If validators differ from the paper's, success rates are not comparable to published baselines; sensitivity: medium — the internal comparison (arm vs. arm) remains valid, but external comparability is lost.
A3. Model API access and cost envelope. If budget is much smaller than assumed, reduce tasks and runs per the power reasoning (prioritize R over task count up to the pairing benefit plateau); sensitivity: medium — determines detectable effect size, not validity.
A4. Deterministic instance seeding. If ServiceNow task instances cannot be re-seeded per run, run-level stochasticity conflates instance variation with decoding variation; sensitivity: medium — the paired task-level analysis still holds, but R should then be interpreted as repeated attempts on identical instances, and run-level variance estimates become conservative.
A5. Validators are automatic and deterministic. If any validator requires human judgment, add an inter-annotator agreement step; sensitivity: low if rare, high if common.
A6. Single scaffold faithfulness. If the available scaffold already embeds internal reasoning (e.g., a built-in "think" field), the no-CoT arm must be constructed by stripping it, and A3's interleaved format must be adapted to it; sensitivity: medium — poor stripping would attenuate the contrast.
A7. Model knowledge of ServiceNow/UI conventions is comparable across arms (it is, since arms share the model — this is guaranteed by design, not assumed).
A8. Task inventory access for stratified sampling; sensitivity: low — sampling scheme degrades gracefully to "all available tasks."

Uncertainties carried forward: exact task counts per family/difficulty in the deployed instance; whether the instance supports per-run reseeding; final API pricing/quota; whether the researcher wants A4 matched to A2 only (default) or to both CoT arms; final model choice(s).

====================================================
9. STATUS
====================================================
This is a design only. No experiment was run, no code was executed beyond read-only workspace inspection, and no results — interim or final — are claimed. Execution would require the resources enumerated in §8 and researcher sign-off on the open decisions in §7 and the uncertainties above.
